title: MIO and Any-to-Any Streaming Multimodal Models

questions.question: What makes an any-to-any model different from a pipeline of separate vision, text, and speech models?
options: Each modality uses a separate model and passes only text to the next.
A speech model converts every input modality into audio first.
One causal transformer consumes and emits interleaved modality tokens.
One image encoder produces captions that are sent to a speech API.
questions.explanation: An any-to-any model tokenizes modalities into one interleaved sequence and uses one causal transformer to condition and generate across them. A pipeline of separate models needs handoffs and can lose information at each conversion.

questions.question: Which tokenizer assignment matches the MIO stack described in the lesson?
options: Text uses SEED, images use BPE, speech uses CLIP, and music uses a VQ text tokenizer.
Speech uses the image encoder, while music uses the text vocabulary.
Text uses BPE, images use SEED, speech uses residual-VQ, and music uses an Encodec-like tokenizer.
Every modality uses the same image VQ tokenizer and one shared codebook.
questions.explanation: MIO uses BPE for text, SEED VQ codes for images, residual-VQ for speech, and an Encodec-family tokenizer for music. One shared image tokenizer would not provide the modality-specific speech and music representations described.

questions.question: What do the later codebooks in speech residual-VQ add after the first coarse content level?
options: Prosody and speaker-identity detail.
Image patch positions and bounding-box coordinates.
Text vocabulary entries and punctuation.
Video frame timestamps and spatial rows.
questions.explanation: Residual-VQ layers refine a coarse speech code: the first level carries content, while later levels add prosody and speaker identity. Image patch positions or video timestamps are not the information those audio codebooks encode.

questions.question: What is the order of MIO's four-stage training curriculum?
options: Alignment, interleaved data, speech-focused training, then instruction tuning.
Interleaved data, alignment, instruction tuning, then speech enhancement.
Instruction tuning, speech enhancement, alignment, then interleaved data.
Alignment, instruction tuning, image generation, then text-only training.
questions.explanation: The curriculum first aligns modality pairs, then trains on interleaved documents, adds speech-focused data, and finally instruction-tunes across modalities. Each stage addresses a different capability, so swapping instruction tuning to the beginning skips alignment/context learning.

questions.question: A speech product needs lower latency after the transformer predicts the base speech stream. Which part does MIO parallel-decode?
options: Residual-VQ levels that add prosody and speaker detail.
The transformer layers that process the incoming audio.
The text BPE sequence that forms the user's prompt.
Every image patch in the shared visual vocabulary.
questions.explanation: The model first predicts the base speech stream; parallel decoding of residual-VQ levels adds prosody and speaker detail without waiting for each level sequentially. Parallel refinement reduces latency while retaining the layered audio representation.

questions.question: Why should modality token IDs occupy disjoint ranges in the shared vocabulary?
options: So every modality can reuse the same integer for unrelated codes.
So text tokens can be sorted after image tokens during decoding.
So each integer ID unambiguously identifies its modality's token.
So the transformer does not need image or speech separators.
questions.explanation: Disjoint ID ranges let the shared embedding/output vocabulary identify whether an integer denotes text, image, speech, or music. Reusing one ID for unrelated codes would make token interpretation ambiguous, even with modality separators.
